hero.description: PULSE measures whether your product data is ready to support the decisions your shoppers are trying to make, ranked, in your own catalogue, in 48 hours. Then it decides what to show, and when one more question is worth their time.

problem.title: 47 of 216 laptops record nothing a shopper could filter on.
problem.body: We took one real merchant catalogue and looked at a single shelf. No screen size. No memory. No storage. No processor. Those specifications are unavailable to anything that depends on structured catalogue attributes, filters cannot use them, guided selling cannot reason over them as explicit fields, and every system downstream has to re-infer what the catalogue should already state.
problem.caption: Often the fact exists, somewhere less useful. Here it is in the title, queryable by nothing. Sometimes it is in a supplier feed nobody mapped. Sometimes it was never recorded at all. The audit tells you which.

how.title: Audit. Enrich. Then decide.
how.body: Personalisation sold on top of a catalogue that records nothing is personalisation that cannot work. We start one step earlier than everyone else.

s1.title: Decision Audit
s1.body: Send one catalogue export. We rank every attribute by how much deciding power it carries today, and how much it would carry if it were recorded everywhere. The gap is what the missing data costs you.
s1.meta: 48 hours · no code · product data only

s2.title: You fix what it points at
s2.body: With the specific products listed. You may not need us for this at all, if your team can populate the top attribute, the audit has paid for itself and you should go and do that.
s2.meta: We also return what we could recover from your existing titles

s3.title: PULSE decides
s3.body: The engine reads the live session, infers what the visitor appears to need, and ranks your catalogue against it, asking a question only when the answer would change what it shows. It runs alongside your store and search; it replaces neither.
s3.meta: no cookies · no login required · runs alongside your store

audit.title: A ranked list of what to record first, in your own products.
audit.body: "Enrich your catalogue" is correct and useless: a catalogue has hundreds of possible fields and nobody can tell you which ones matter. So it becomes an unbounded project, it gets deprioritised, and every discovery tool on top of it keeps underperforming for a reason nobody names.
audit.callout: Look at Processor. It contributes almost nothing today, which is exactly why a catalogue review by eye would dismiss it. Under the same decision model it is the third-highest repair priority, because 162 products are missing it. That is easy to miss when you are reviewing completeness percentages alone.

table.caption: Decision Audit, laptops
table.foot: Measured in bits of decision information, not revenue, not conversions. On a real 216-product shelf, reproducible from the repository (ODIN/research/SPIKE-VOI.md §9.4).

proof.title: Choosing the question beats asking every question.

m1.label: PULSE, mean
m1.foot: Against 4.00 for a fixed questionnaire, the model every guided-selling product uses. A 29% reduction.

m2.label: Unaskable products
m2.foot: Record no attribute a shopper could filter on, so they survive every question. After every question this shelf can support, a shopper is still choosing between 94 products on average.

m3.label: Inferred live
m3.foot: Gender, age, skin tone, undertone, each a calibrated distribution, derived from catalogue statistics rather than assigned.

honesty.title: What these numbers do not establish
honesty.body: This is a search-efficiency measurement against a known answer. It says nothing about whether shoppers would answer a question, and nothing about revenue. We have no measured commercial uplift, because we have not run a pilot with a control group yet. When we have one, it will be from your traffic, not someone else's store.

about.title: We start one step
about.description: Every discovery vendor assumes the catalogue already records what the product is. We checked, on a real merchant's shelf, and it does not, so we built the measurement that says which missing field costs the most, and we sell that before we sell anything else.

mission.title: What we are for
mission.description: PULSE helps stores decide when they know enough to recommend, and when one more question is worth the shopper's time. Before either is possible, the catalogue has to be able to answer the question at all, and almost nobody checks whether it can.

problem.title: What we found
problem.description: We asked how many questions a shopper would need to answer before we could confidently show them the right laptop. The answer was none, ever: 47 of the 216 products on the shelf record nothing a shopper could filter on, so they survive every question and the shelf can never be narrowed. The specifications were not missing, they were sitting inside the product titles, where no filter can reach them.

solution.title: What we built instead
solution.description: We could have shipped the question engine anyway and shown a good demo. Instead we recorded that the catalogue defeats it, and built the measurement that ranks which missing attribute costs the most decisions. That became the Decision Audit, the thing a merchant can act on in a week, with no integration and no code.

privacy.title: Inference over identity
privacy.description: The engine reads the current visit. No login, no cookie, no profile to look up, so there is nothing to leak and nothing to get consent for between visits.

innovation.title: Arithmetic over rules
innovation.description: Poor data should weaken a signal by itself, not because someone tuned a constant. A category with no evidence contributes exactly zero, and that falls out of the maths.

results.title: Measured or labelled
results.description: Every number we publish is either measured, with a source, or marked as not measured. We fixed our success criteria before running the spike, and when they turned out to be insufficient we said so rather than rewriting them.

customer.title: Useful before contracted
customer.description: The audit is designed to be worth acting on whether or not the merchant ever works with us. If their own team can populate the top attribute, they should go and do that.

team.title: The team
team.description: A small team in Ho Chi Minh City. The engine is built on this market first, population priors, urban sex ratios by city, VND price bands, Vietnamese text handling down to đ normalisation, because that is a head start a foreign entrant would not build first.

ml.title: Inference

items.question: Why is there no free tier or price list?
items.answer: Because we are early and every pilot is scoped by hand. A published rate card would imply a repeatable product motion we have not earned yet. Pricing is agreed per pilot, in writing, before anything starts.

items.question: What does the audit actually cost me if it finds nothing?
items.answer: A catalogue export and a fixed fee. If the audit says your catalogue is fine, it says so, and you have spent very little to learn that discovery is not your bottleneck. That is a useful answer.

items.question: We already have search and recommendations. Does this replace them?
items.answer: No, keep them. They read the same catalogue fields we do, which is why the audit helps them too. If screen size is not recorded, your search facets cannot offer it either.

items.question: Isn't this just data cleanup?
items.answer: Data cleanup is unbounded. This is a ranked, finite list of the fields that change outcomes, with the products attached. The difference is knowing when to stop.

items.question: How is this different from a PIM?
items.answer: Keep your PIM. A PIM is where product information is governed, enriched and distributed, that is not what we do. PULSE adds a different question: given the buying decisions your catalogue has to support, what should you improve first? We hand that priority list back to whatever already manages your product data. If you run Akeneo, Salsify, Productsup or your own system, the audit is an input to it, not a replacement for it.

items.question: Will you quote us an uplift percentage?
items.answer: Not before we have measured one on your traffic. We do not have a measured revenue result from a live merchant yet, and anyone who gives you a number before running the test is quoting someone else's store.

overview.title: How It Works
overview.intro: Pulse personalizes your storefront in three moves: capture anonymous in-session signals, tell us what you sell, then ask us how to order it for the visitor in front of you. The browser SDK handles the first; your backend handles the other two over a simple REST API.
overview.step1Desc: Drop in the SDK. It quietly streams anonymous behavior to Pulse in the background. No cookies, nothing personal.
overview.step2Desc: Push your products and categories so Pulse knows what it can recommend and rank.
overview.step3Desc: Call the Personalization API to reorder grids and search results for the live visitor.

auth.title: Authentication
auth.signupNote: You'll need a Pulse account first. Sign up to create your organization, then generate and manage your API keys from the dashboard.
auth.signupCta: Sign up to get your API keys →
auth.intro: All API requests require authentication using an API key. Include your key in the Authorization header.
auth.securityNote: Never expose your secret API key in client-side code. All inference and catalog requests should be made from your backend servers. The browser SDK uses a publishable key (pk_live_…) scoped to event ingestion only.

inference.title: Inference API
inference.desc: Get real-time persona inference for a visitor session. Returns persona attributes, confidence scores, and recommended product rankings.

catalog.title: Catalog Sync, Products & Categories
catalog.intro: Push your products and categories to Pulse so the engine knows what it can personalize. Send a full catalog once, then keep it in sync by sending each create, update, or delete as it happens in your store.
catalog.async: Enrichment and Digital Twin tagging run asynchronously in the ingestion pipeline, the upsert call returns 202 Accepted immediately and the products.tagged webhook fires when a product becomes available for inference. Inference itself stays on the request path.
catalog.upsertDesc: Create or update products. The call is idempotent on id, send the same product again with new fields to update it. Accepts one product or a batch.
catalog.categoriesDesc: Sync your category tree so Pulse understands how products relate. Set parent_id to mirror your store's hierarchy. Upserted the same way as products.
catalog.deleteDesc: Remove a product when it is deleted or permanently out of stock. It stops appearing in recommendations immediately. Use the same pattern to delete categories.
catalog.syncNote: Most merchants wire these calls to their store's product/category change events (e.g. a Shopify webhook or a save hook in a custom backend) so the Pulse catalog always mirrors what shoppers see. A nightly full re-sync is recommended as a safety net.

personalize.title: Personalization API
personalize.desc: Once the SDK is capturing signals and your catalog is synced, call these endpoints to reorder your storefront in real time for the current visitor. Call them from your backend with a Bearer token, passing the session_id the SDK created in the browser.
personalize.recommendDesc: Return a ranked list of products personalized to the visitor's live persona, use it for "For You" grids, related products, and homepage rails.
personalize.searchDesc: Re-rank your search results by intent. Send the shopper's query and Pulse orders the matching products by the persona inferred this session. Results are cursor-paginated.

webhooks.title: Webhooks
webhooks.intro: Configure webhooks to receive real-time notifications for events like persona updates, conversion tracking, and model improvements.

errors.title: Errors
errors.intro: Pulse uses standard HTTP status codes and returns errors in the RFC 7807 Problem Details format, so every error includes a machine-readable type and a human-readable detail.
errors.e400: Bad Request, the payload is malformed or a required field is missing.
errors.e401: Unauthorized, the API key is missing or invalid.
errors.e403: Forbidden, the key is valid but not permitted for this resource.
errors.e404: Not Found, the session, product, or endpoint does not exist.
errors.e422: Unprocessable Entity, the request is well-formed but fails validation.
errors.e429: Too Many Requests, you have exceeded your plan's rate limit.
errors.e500: Server Error, something went wrong on our side; retry with backoff.

product.title: The system that knows what it
product.description: Every recommendation is a bet made under uncertainty. Most engines hide that; ours measures it, names where the uncertainty lives, and closes the gap the cheapest way available, which is sometimes a question, and more often a product field nobody recorded.

gaps.title: Three gaps, closed in order
gaps.description: They are not equally hard, and they are not equally finished. The table says which is which, including the two we have not built yet.

items.how: Tell the merchant which attributes to record, ranked by decision impact, with the affected products listed.
Infer from behaviour in the current visit; ask only when the answer would change the decision.
Separate verified fact from inference, with provenance, so an AI shopping agent can tell them apart.

gaps.foot: We sell the first. The second and third are why the first is not a consulting engagement.

pipeline.title: What happens in a visit
pipeline.description: No login, no cookie, no profile to look up. Five steps, running alongside your store rather than in front of it.

steps.title: Visitor
steps.desc: Arrives anonymously. There is nothing to look up and nothing to match against.

steps.title: Signals
steps.desc: Scroll, dwell, search terms, category opens and filter use, the current visit only.

steps.title: Distributions
steps.desc: Each named dimension updated by likelihood ratio, starting from the visitor's own population.

steps.title: Ranking
steps.desc: Your catalogue scored against the distributions, with audience fit as one weighted term.

steps.title: Decision
steps.desc: Show, re-rank, or ask, a question only when its answer would change the ranking.

inference.title: Inference you can argue with

ourAudit.title: The audit we sell, run on our own site
ourAudit.lede: A Decision Audit asks what a visitor is trying to decide, then measures whether the content can resolve it. Here is that measurement applied to this site, computed from the page catalogue at build time rather than written by hand.
ourAudit.finding: The distribution is the shape of a site written by the people who built the product: heavy on what the authors find interesting, thin on what the decision needs. That is the same failure as a catalogue that records colour and omits the processor.
ourAudit.method: Information value is how much resolving a requirement is worth, in bits: a requirement that many pages answer is nearly free to satisfy, and one that a single page answers is the bottleneck of the visit. It is computed, not assigned.
caveats: Coverage is not quality. A page that declares it resolves a requirement may still resolve it badly, and nothing here measures that.
The counts move whenever a page is added, including this one. They are derived at build time rather than quoted from a report.
A requirement no page resolves would not appear at all, which is the same survivorship blind spot we warn merchants about. The vocabulary is fixed in advance for exactly that reason.
